abstract: |
  **Background:** Despite growing policy commitments to open data sharing, little empirical evidence exists on the day-to-day operational realities of coordinating large-scale health research data sharing. Understanding what this work actually involves is essential for designing realistic and equitable governance frameworks, and for planning and appropriately resourcing data-sharing operations.\
  **Methods:** This study analyzes 6,833 emails from the inbox of a central operations manager at the Canadian COVID-19 Immunity Task Force (CITF) Databank, spanning correspondence with 100 partnering studies and 491 unique senders from February 2021 to September 2025. Emails were preprocessed using rule-based cleaning and automated de-identification. Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) was applied for topic modeling, selecting k = 14 topics based on coherence, granularity, and topic diversity, with topic labels and thematic groupings generated using a locally deployed large language model. Topic distribution was analyzed across five lifecycle phases, five sender roles, and the gender of senders, and within-study topic co-occurrence was examined to characterize how workstreams combined. All analyses report per-study median values to neutralize the influence of high-volume studies and individual senders.\
  **Results:** The 14 topics fell into four thematic categories, namely Agreements and Contracts, Data Operations, Study Documentation, and Coordination. Agreements topics peaked in early lifecycle phases while Data Operations topics peaked progressively later, with Serology and Data Harmonization reaching a median share of 55% during the final phase. Among studies that reached both bounding milestones, the negotiation phase (median 395 days) and the data preparation phase (median 398 days) were the longest, while technical cataloguing was only 22 days. Sender roles showed distinct topical territories, with External Partners specializing in agreements, the Databank Harmonization Group in study documentation, and the Databank Secretariat serving as connective tissue across every workstream. Although women constituted 64.5% of unique senders, they were systematically under-represented in Data Operations topics (28.6% to 51.8% women-share, 12.8 to 36 percentage points below baseline) and in Agreements topics (46.2% to 57.1%, 7.5 to 18.5 percentage points below baseline), while over-representation in Study Documentation was milder (around 7 percentage points above baseline). Within-study topic co-occurrence revealed two largely separate clusters, with Agreements topics travelling together (top pairs at 25 to 33% within-study coupling) and Data Operations integrating tightly with Study Documentation (top pair at 35.3%) but rarely with Agreements (mostly 0 to 5%).\
  **Conclusions:** Data sharing coordination is primarily an administrative and governance challenge rather than a technical one. The four analyses converge on a single structural finding, that agreements work and technical data work run as parallel rather than integrated workstreams within studies, differentiated temporally, by role, by gender, and by within-study topic co-occurrence. These findings have direct implications for how Canadian research data infrastructure is resourced, governed, and staffed under national policy frameworks, particularly as institutions build capacity to meet Tri-Agency Research Data Management obligations.
